walkthroughs.body_html:
Kinematics — a core area of A-Level Maths.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Kinematics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Kinematics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A particle starts from rest and accelerates at 4 m/s² for 3 seconds. Final velocity is:
options: 12 m/s
7 m/s

mcqs.q: Which SUVAT equation does NOT involve t?
options: v² = u² + 2as
v = u + at
s = ut + ½at²

mcqs.q: Can a definite integral give a negative value, even when integrating a function from left to right?
options: Definite integrals are always positive because area cannot be negative.
Definite integrals are negative only when the limits are reversed.
Only on equilateral triangles because all sides are equal.
Yes — if the function is below the x-axis over the interval, the integral is negative.

mcqs.q: Can Pythagoras' theorem be used on any triangle?
options: No — it only applies to right-angled triangles.
Yes — it works on any triangle as long as you square the sides.
Only on equilateral triangles because all sides are equal.
Definite integrals are negative only when the limits are reversed.

mcqs.q: Is the result of 6 / 0.5 larger or smaller than 6?
options: Smaller, because division always makes numbers smaller.
Only on equilateral triangles because all sides are equal.
Equal to 6, because 0.5 is half and so cancels out.
Larger — dividing by a number less than 1 gives a bigger result (6 / 0.5 = 12).

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Vertical motion under gravity”?
options: Slope = acceleration; area under graph = displacement. Helpful for visualising motion.
Take a = g = 9.8 m/s² downward (or 9.81). Use SUVAT for projectiles, free fall.
For constant acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ((u+v)/2)t. Useful when a is constant.
Speed is scalar (magnitude of velocity). Velocity is vector — has direction.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Displacement, velocity, acceleration”?
options: Take a = g = 9.8 m/s² downward (or 9.81). Use SUVAT for projectiles, free fall.
If a depends on t: v = ∫a dt; s = ∫v dt. Use calculus rather than SUVAT.
Displacement s (vector); velocity v = ds/dt; acceleration a = dv/dt = d²s/dt². All are vectors in 2D/3D.
Speed is scalar (magnitude of velocity). Velocity is vector — has direction.

options: Speed is scalar (magnitude of velocity). Velocity is vector — has direction.
Take a = g = 9.8 m/s² downward (or 9.81). Use SUVAT for projectiles, free fall.

For constant acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ((u+v)/2)t. Useful when a is constant.
